usage: polite; opens your view to anyone
반말; to a friend or younger person
the way I see it / from my perspective
slightly more formal variant — emphasizes the angle, not just the thought
제 생각에는 좀 다른 것 같아요
I think it's a bit different
natural extension that softens disagreement while staying polite
examples: 제 생각에는 이 방법이 더 빠를 것 같아요.
In my opinion, this method might be faster.
basic use: the opener leads into a hedged recommendation with -ㄹ 것 같다
A: 어떤 색이 더 잘 어울려요? / B: 제 생각에는 파란색이 훨씬 자연스럽게 보여요.
A: Which color suits me better? / B: In my opinion, the blue looks much more natural.
A/B exchange: B uses 제 생각에는 to give a personal aesthetic judgment without sounding pushy
제 생각에는 이 방법도 좋지만, 비용 면에서 좀 더 따져봐야 할 것 같아요.
In my opinion this approach is fine too, but I think we need to look more carefully at costs.
fuller discussion turn: agrees in part, then raises a concern — shows the phrase opens a nuanced view, not just simple agreement
nuance: 제 생각에는 is the standard polite opener that signals 'this is just my view, not a command or fact'. 제 is the humble form of 나 ('my'), and 에는 sets up a frame — literally 'as for within my thinking'. It works with anyone: strangers, seniors, classmates, colleagues, customers. To go casual with a close friend, swap to 내 생각에는; for a more considered, slightly formal feel use 제 생각으로는 (the -으로는 particle stresses the viewpoint angle). The nearest alternative is 제가 보기에는 — the dividing line is thinking vs observing: 제 생각에는 comes from your internal reasoning, while 제가 보기에는 is based on what you see or sense from evidence. The classic English-speaker mistake is calquing 'in my opinion' literally as 제 의견에는, which is bookish and rare in spoken Korean. A second trap: dropping the particle entirely (제 생각 좋아요) — without 에는 or 엔 the opener is ungrammatical.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '제(my/humble) 생각(thought) 에는(as for within)' → 실제 뜻: 'in my opinion / I think...'. It frames what follows as personal view, not fact — a politeness device as much as a meaning marker. Works with anyone in polite speech.
적절한 격식: 존댓말 (제 생각에는), 반말 (내 생각에는). 격식체: 제 생각으로는 (meetings, written). 친구에게 제 생각에는 쓰면 지나치게 격식적으로 들린다 — 내 생각에는이 훨씬 자연스럽다.

제가 보기에는 is the nearest neighbor. 제 생각에는 = internal reasoning ('I figure/think'); 제가 보기에는 = observation-based judgment ('from what I see'). A second near-synonym is 제 입장에서는 ('from my position/standpoint'), which stresses situational perspective over pure opinion.
더 세게: 솔직히 제 생각에는 ('honestly, in my opinion'). 더 부드럽게: 제 생각에는 그런 것 같아요 (adds -것 같아요 hedge). 과거 상황: 제 생각에는 그게 맞는 것 같았는데요 ('I thought at the time that was right').

1) 제 의견에는 — a literal calque that sounds stiff and bookish; spoken Korean uses 제 생각에는. 2) 생각에 (dropping 는) — weakens the topic frame; keep 에는 or at minimum 에는 → 엔 in fast speech. 3) Using 제 생각에는 with a close friend — drop to 내 생각에는 so you don't sound overly formal.

mistakes: Saying 제 의견에는 as a literal translation of 'in my opinion' — it sounds bookish; natural speech uses 제 생각에는.
Using 제 생각에는 with a friend — it's polite register; with friends drop to 반말: 내 생각에는.
Omitting the particle (제 생각 좋아요) — you need 제 생각에는 / 제 생각엔; the bare noun can't open the clause this way.

english: The way I see it / From what I can tell...
usage: polite; offering a judgment from observation
same meaning, more conversational; very common in spoken Korean
제가 보기에는 별문제 없을 것 같아요
from what I can see, I don't think there'll be a problem
full reassuring judgment based on what you've observed
examples: 제가 보기에는 괜찮은데요.
From what I can see, it looks fine.
bare judgment, softened by -는데요 which invites the listener's take
A: 이 지원자 어떻게 보세요? / B: 제가 보기에는 경험이 부족한 것 같아요.
A: What do you make of this applicant? / B: The way I see it, they seem a bit short on experience.
A/B exchange: B gives an observation-based assessment in a professional context where 보기에는 is very natural
제가 보기에는 가격은 비슷한데 품질 면에서는 이쪽이 확실히 낫네요.
The way I see it, the price is similar but this one is clearly better in terms of quality.
fuller real opinion weighing two options from visible evidence
nuance: 제가 보기에는 means 'judging from what I observe/see', used when you give an assessment rooted in visible evidence or your read of a situation — polite, works with anyone. The grammar is 보다 ('to see') + -기 (nominalizer) + 에는, literally 'as for in my seeing'. The casual form is 내가 보기에는; the contracted 제가 보기엔 is extremely common in natural speech. The nearest neighbor is 제 생각에는 — the dividing line is evidence vs reasoning: 제가 보기에는 says 'based on observable signs' (appearance, behavior, data), while 제 생각에는 expresses your internal reasoning or opinion independent of direct observation. For pure feelings ('I feel nervous') neither works — state the feeling directly. English speakers often say 제가 봤을 때 ('when I looked', a specific past moment) when they mean the general present-tense judgment 제가 보기에는; keep it present and nominalized.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '제가(I) 보기(the act of seeing) 에는(as for)' → 실제 뜻: 'from what I can see / the way I see it'. It grounds the judgment in observation — if you just went from gut feeling alone, 제 생각에는 fits better.
적절한 격식: 존댓말 (제가 보기에는), 반말 (내가 보기에는). 격식: 제가 보기에는/제가 보기엔 모두 polite setting에서 자연스럽다. 직장 선배나 처음 만난 사람에게도 쓸 수 있다. 친구에게는 내가 보기에는 또는 줄여서 내가 보기엔.

제 생각에는 vs 제가 보기에는: 생각에는 = inner reasoning; 보기에는 = outward observation. A third near-synonym is 제 느낌에는 ('from my sense/feel'), which is even more subjective and emotional — use it for gut feelings rather than visible evidence.
기본: 제가 보기에는. 단축: 제가 보기엔 (very common in speech). 반말: 내가 보기에는 / 내가 보기엔. 강조: 솔직히 제가 보기에는... 완화: 제가 보기엔 좀 그런 것 같아요 (adds -것 같아요 to soften further).

1) 제가 봤을 때 (past 'when I looked') vs 제가 보기에는 (general present judgment) — don't use the past form for a general assessment. 2) Dropping 가: 제 보기에는 is ungrammatical — the subject marker 가 is obligatory. 3) Using it for emotions: '제가 보기에는 무서워요' is odd; for feelings, just say 무서워요 or 제 생각에는 무서운 것 같아요.

mistakes: Confusing it with 제가 봤을 때 ('when I saw it', a specific past moment) — for a general read use the present 제가 보기에는.
Saying 제 보기에는 without 가 — the subject marker is needed: 제가 보기에는.
Using it for pure feelings ('I feel sad') — 보기에는 is for judgments/assessments, not emotions; for feelings use 제 생각에는 or just state the feeling.

usage: polite agreement/factual confirmation; works with anyone
반말; to a close friend or someone younger
격식체; announcements, customer service, work presentations
doubled for enthusiastic agreement; very common in conversation as a back-channel signal
examples: A: 이 길로 가면 돼요? / B: 네, 맞아요.
A: Do we go this way? / B: Yes, that's right.
A/B exchange: B confirms a factual claim; the most common single-word confirmation in everyday Korean
맞아요, 저도 어제 그 기사 봤어요. 진짜 충격적이더라고요.
Right, I saw that article yesterday too. It was really shocking.
agreeing and chaining your own experience; -더라고요 reports what you personally discovered
아, 맞아요! 그 카페 주말엔 오후 다섯 시에 문 닫더라고요. 저도 그냥 돌아왔었어요.
Oh, that's right! That cafe closes at 5 PM on weekends. I turned back empty-handed too.
recalling a fact with -더라고요 and sharing a personal story that confirms the point
nuance: 맞아요 comes from 맞다, which originally means 'to fit / to be correct', and it confirms that what the other person said is factually accurate — the Korean equivalent of 'right, exactly'. It's polite and works with anyone; casual is 맞아; formal is 맞습니다. The nearest alternative is 그렇죠 / 그래요 — the dividing line is precision: 맞아요 judges a specific statement as correct or accurate (like a fact check), while 그렇죠 is a warmer, more empathetic 'yeah, that's how it is' that builds conversational rapport rather than verifying truth. The biggest English-speaker trap is treating 맞아요 as 'okay / sure' for agreeing to requests — for 'okay, I'll do it' you need 알겠어요 or 좋아요. A second trap is answering negative questions: if someone asks 안 더워요? ('isn't it hot?'), a flat 맞아요 is confusing; Koreans typically answer the embedded proposition. Grammatically, 맞다 is intransitive here — 맞아요 stands alone as a complete reply; do not combine it with 하다.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 맞다 = 'to fit/be correct' → 실제 뜻: 'that's right / you're correct'. 맞아요 is a factual confirmation: it says the thing the other person stated is accurate. It does NOT simply express enthusiasm or assent to a request.

존댓말: 맞아요 (anyone — friend's parent, teacher, customer, coworker). 반말: 맞아 (close friend, younger person). 격식: 맞습니다 (business presentation, customer service reply, formal announcement). 가장 자연스러운 상황: 누군가가 사실을 말하거나 방향/정보를 확인할 때.

맞아요 vs 그렇죠: 맞아요 = 'that statement is correct' (factual); 그렇죠 = 'yeah, that's the way it is' (empathetic/rapport-building). In casual chat, 그렇죠 often sounds warmer; use 맞아요 when you're actually verifying accuracy.
단독: 맞아요 / 맞아. 강조: 맞아요, 맞아요 (doubled = emphatic). 격식: 맞습니다. 과거 확인: 맞았어요 ('that was right'). 관형어: 맞는 말이에요 ('that's the right/correct thing to say').

1) Using 맞아요 to mean 'okay, I'll do it' — for consent to a request say 알겠어요 or 좋아요. 2) Conjugating it 맞어요 — the stem vowel is ㅏ, so it must be 맞아요, not 맞어요. 3) Answering a negative question (안 ~요?) with 맞아요 — this is ambiguous; restate the proposition clearly.

mistakes: Using 맞아요 to mean 'okay, I'll do that' — for agreeing to a request say 알겠어요 or 좋아요; 맞아요 only confirms correctness.
Writing 맞어요 — the conjugation of 맞다 is 맞아요 (ㅏ stem), not 맞어요.
Saying 맞아요를 해요 or adding 하다 — 맞다 already is the verb; 맞아요 is a complete reply.

usage: polite; seeking or giving warm, shared agreement
반말; to a friend — same meaning, same warmth
격식체; formal confirmation in presentations or service settings
rising tone to invite the listener to agree with YOUR statement; a tag-question equivalent
examples: 요즘 진짜 피곤하죠? — 그렇죠, 요즘 일이 너무 많아요.
It's really exhausting lately, right? — Exactly, there's just too much work.
A/B exchange: B uses 그렇죠 to echo the feeling and validate it, building rapport
그렇죠. 그래서 제가 미리 확인해 뒀어요.
Right, exactly — that's why I checked ahead of time.
falling tone: agreeing with what was just said, then showing you acted on that shared understanding
그렇죠, 사실 저도 처음엔 좀 망설였는데 막상 해보니까 괜찮더라고요.
Right, honestly I hesitated at first too, but once I actually tried it, it was fine.
agreeing, adding personal context, then sharing a nuancing discovery
nuance: 그렇죠 comes from 그렇다 ('to be so') + the ending 죠, which is a contraction of 지요. The -지요 ending uniquely seeks mutual confirmation or shared understanding — it says 'you'd agree, right?' — making 그렇죠 feel warm and socially connective rather than merely factual. This is the key distinction from 맞아요: 맞아요 verifies a fact as correct; 그렇죠 says 'yeah, we're on the same page / that's how life is'. Casual is 그렇지; formal is 그렇습니다. With a rising tone (그렇죠?) it becomes a tag question inviting the listener to confirm your view. A common near-synonym is 그래요 — 그렇죠 is slightly more emphatic and warmer, nudging for agreement; 그래요 is a neutral 'yes, that's right'. English speakers often miss this warmth and reach for the more transactional 맞아요 everywhere; in small talk and emotional sharing, 그렇죠 is the more natural choice. Watch the spelling: the stem is 그렇다, so keep the ㅎ — it's 그렇죠, not 그러죠.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 그렇다(to be so) + 죠(지요 contracted) → 실제 뜻: 'that's how it is, right?' The -죠 ending is the key: it creates mutual ground, not just factual confirmation — it says 'we both know this is true'. That warmth sets it apart from bare 그래요.
존댓말: 그렇죠. 반말: 그렇지. 격식: 그렇습니다. 상황: 소소한 일상 대화, 상대방의 말에 공감할 때, 자기 말에 상대의 동의를 구할 때 (그렇죠? 질문형). 상사나 고객에게도 자연스럽다.

맞아요 vs 그렇죠: 맞아요 = 'that statement is factually correct'; 그렇죠 = 'yeah, that's how things are / we're aligned'. 그래요 vs 그렇죠: 그래요 is neutral agreement; 그렇죠 is warmer and more emphatic, actively pulling the other person into shared understanding.
평서: 그렇죠 (falling tone = 'exactly'). 의문: 그렇죠? (rising tone = 'isn't it?'). 반말: 그렇지 / 그렇지? 격식: 그렇습니다. 강조: 맞죠, 그렇죠? (stacking for extra emphasis).

1) 맞아요 everywhere — 그렇죠 is warmer and more natural in small talk and emotional sharing. 2) Spelling 그러죠 — the stem keeps ㅎ: 그렇죠. 3) Treating 죠 as casual — 죠/지요 is polite (contains 요 level); casual is 그렇지.

mistakes: Spelling it 그러죠 — the stem is 그렇다, so it keeps ㅎ: 그렇죠.
Using 그렇죠 to correct a factual claim — for 'that's the correct answer' use 맞아요; 그렇죠 is empathetic agreement.
Treating the ending 죠 as casual — 죠/지요 is polite (it contains 요); the casual version is 그렇지 without 요.

usage: polite; slightly formal, natural in discussions, meetings, or reacting to an opinion
반말; to a friend or peer in a relaxed setting
격식체; presentations, debates, official decisions — the expected form in business Korean
I agree with that opinion too
extension naming what you agree with; note the particle 에
examples: 네, 저도 동의해요. 그게 훨씬 합리적인 것 같아요.
Yes, I agree. That seems much more reasonable.
polite agreement followed by a reason — the reason softens and substantiates the agreement
A: 이번 계획을 좀 더 구체화해야 할 것 같아요. / B: 동의해요. 일정표를 먼저 잡는 게 좋겠어요.
A: I think we need to flesh out this plan a bit more. / B: I agree. We should lock down a schedule first.
A/B meeting exchange: B uses 동의해요 then adds a concrete next step — natural in Korean work discussions
전반적으로는 동의하는데, 예산 부분만 좀 더 검토가 필요할 것 같아요.
I agree overall, but I think the budget section needs a bit more review.
agrees in principle, then politely raises a reservation — the -는데 (but) pivot is key
nuance: 동의해요 comes from 동의[同意], the Sino-Korean word for 'agreement of intent/purpose', plus 해요. It is the slightly formal, discussion-register way to say 'I agree' — comfortable with anyone in meetings, class, or when reacting to a proposal or argument. For casual friend chat it can feel stiff; 맞아 or 나도 그렇게 생각해 are more natural there. Casual is 동의해; formal is 동의합니다 (standard in business settings). The nearest everyday alternative is 저도 그렇게 생각해요 — the dividing line: 동의해요 signals 'I endorse this position', closer to a formal agreement vote; 저도 그렇게 생각해요 is a warmer 'I feel the same way'. A related word is 동감이에요 ('I share the feeling') — 동감 is emotional resonance; 동의 is intellectual assent. The most common English-speaker error is the particle: you agree WITH something using 에 (그 의견에 동의해요), not 을/를 — English 'agree with' misleads learners into using the object marker.

structuredNuance.t: 直譯: 동의[同意](same intention/agreement) + 해요 → 실제 뜻: 'I endorse this position / I agree'. It is more deliberate and formal than a casual 맞아 — you're aligning yourself with a stated stance or argument, not just nodding.
존댓말: 동의해요 (meetings, class, semi-formal discussion). 반말: 동의해 (peers, friends — but can still feel a bit bookish). 격식: 동의합니다 (business presentations, formal votes). 친구들끼리: 맞아 / 나도 그렇게 생각해가 더 자연스럽다.

동의해요 vs 저도 그렇게 생각해요: 동의해요 = 'I endorse the position' (intellectual, slightly formal); 저도 그렇게 생각해요 = 'I feel/think the same' (warmer, conversational). 동의해요 vs 동감이에요: 동의 = intellectual agreement with a statement; 동감 = emotional resonance/shared feeling.
기본: 동의해요. 강조: 완전히 동의해요 ('I completely agree'). 격식: 동의합니다. 부분 동의: 어느 정도는 동의해요 ('I agree to some extent'). 부정: 동의하지 않아요 / 동의 못 해요.

1) 그 의견을 동의해요 (wrong particle) — 동의하다 takes 에: 그 의견에 동의해요. English 'agree with' misleads into 을/를. 2) Using 동의해요 in casual friend chat — too bookish; friends say 맞아 or 나도 그렇게 생각해. 3) Confusing 동의 with 동감 — 동감이에요 stresses shared feeling; 동의해요 stresses endorsing a position.

mistakes: Saying 그 의견을 동의해요 — 동의하다 takes 에, not 을/를: 그 의견에 동의해요.
Using 동의해요 in casual friend chat — it sounds formal; friends say 맞아 or 나도 그렇게 생각해.
Confusing 동의 with 동감 — 동감이에요 ('I feel the same') stresses shared feeling; 동의해요 stresses agreeing with a stated position.

usage: polite; the warm everyday way to echo someone's opinion
반말; to a close friend or peer
polished near-synonym; slightly more literary but common in written and semi-formal speech
examples: A: 이 식당 분위기가 참 좋죠? / B: 저도 그렇게 생각해요. 또 오고 싶어요.
A: This restaurant has a great vibe, right? / B: I think so too. I want to come back.
A/B exchange: B echoes the feeling and adds their own desire — the most natural way to agree about atmosphere or impressions
맞아요, 저도 그렇게 생각해요. 지금 바로 결정하기엔 이른 것 같아요.
Right, I think so too. I think it's a bit early to decide right now.
agreeing with a caution and restating the shared hesitation
사실 저도 그렇게 생각했어요. 근데 막상 써 보니까 생각보다 훨씬 편하더라고요.
Honestly I thought so too. But when I actually used it, it was way more convenient than I expected.
past tense form: agreeing about a former view, then pivoting to a surprising discovery — shows the phrase works in narrative
nuance: 저도 그렇게 생각해요 ('I too think like that') is the warm, conversational default for agreeing with someone's opinion — used with anyone in polite speech, and a natural filler for building rapport. Each part carries weight: 저도 = 'I too / me too'; 그렇게 = 'like that / in that way'; 생각해요 = 'think'. Casual is 나도 그렇게 생각해; formal is 저도 그렇게 생각합니다. The nearest alternatives are 동의해요 (more formal, argument-based) and 저도 같은 생각이에요 (a touch more polished, common in semi-formal writing). The most frequent English-speaker mistake is dropping 그렇게 — 저도 생각해요 means only 'I think too' without the 'like that', leaving the sentence incomplete. A second issue: 저도 already encodes 'too/also', so adding 또 or 역시 on top creates redundancy. This phrase is versatile for both facts and feelings, making it the go-to opinionating phrase in everyday Korean.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 저도(I too) 그렇게(like that) 생각해요(think) → 실제 뜻: 'I think so too'. 그렇게 is load-bearing — it refers back to what the other person just said. Drop it and the sentence breaks.
존댓말: 저도 그렇게 생각해요 (누구에게나). 반말: 나도 그렇게 생각해 (친구, 동생). 격식: 저도 그렇게 생각합니다 (회의, 발표). 가장 자연스러운 맥락: 상대가 의견을 말한 뒤 공감을 표현할 때.

저도 그렇게 생각해요 vs 동의해요: 생각해요 = warm, conversational, opinion-based; 동의해요 = formal, intellectual, endorsing a position. 저도 그렇게 생각해요 vs 저도 같은 생각이에요: 같은 생각이에요 is slightly more polished and common in writing, but means the same thing.
약한 동의: 저도 그런 것 같아요 ('I think so too' — hedged). 강한 동의: 저도 정말 그렇게 생각해요 / 완전히 같은 생각이에요. 과거: 저도 그렇게 생각했어요 (I thought so too). 의문: 혹시 저도 그렇게 생각하는 게 맞나요? (seeking validation).

1) 저도 생각해요 (dropping 그렇게) — incomplete; means only 'I think too' without referent. 그렇게 is required. 2) 저도 또 그렇게 생각해요 — redundant; 저도 already means 'too'. 3) Using polite 저도 form in casual chat — with friends swap to 반말: 나도 그렇게 생각해.

mistakes: Dropping 그렇게 (저도 생각해요) — that means only 'I think too' and is incomplete; you need 저도 그렇게 생각해요.
Using polite 저도 그렇게 생각해요 in casual chat — with friends drop to 반말: 나도 그렇게 생각해.
Adding a redundant 또 ('also') — 저도 already means 'me too'; 저도 또 그렇게 생각해요 is doubled.

usage: polite; hedging, stalling, or gently declining — the universal pause in Korean
반말; to a friend — same function, no 요
softened extension that adds honesty; -는데요 at the end keeps it open
trailing pause to signal deep uncertainty or a polite implicit 'no' — the listener reads the hesitation
examples: 주말에 시간 돼요? — 글쎄요, 일정을 한번 확인해 봐야 할 것 같아요.
Are you free this weekend? — Hmm, I'll have to check my schedule.
A/B exchange: B uses 글쎄요 to hedge on a request without a flat refusal — the polite way to buy time
글쎄요. 그게 정말 좋은 생각인지 잘 모르겠어요.
Well... I'm honestly not sure that's a good idea.
expressing genuine doubt about a proposal politely
글쎄요, 그건 좀 더 생각해 봐야 할 것 같아요. 장단점이 있는 것 같아서요.
Well, I think I need to think about that a bit more. It seems to have pros and cons.
buying time before committing to an opinion, then adding a brief rationale
nuance: 글쎄요 is the go-to hedge when you don't want to commit: 'hmm, I'm not sure / let me think / I have reservations'. It works with anyone in polite speech. Unlike 잘 모르겠어요 (which honestly reports ignorance of a fact), 글쎄요 is attitudinal — it expresses hesitation, doubt, reluctance, or a softened refusal. This means Koreans often use it to decline something or avoid a direct 'no' without seeming blunt; the listener is expected to read the hint. Casual is 글쎄. The nearest alternative is 잘 모르겠어요 — the dividing line: 잘 모르겠어요 says 'I genuinely lack this information'; 글쎄요 says 'I'm unsure or noncommittal about the situation'. In a work context where a boss asks a pointed question, 글쎄요 can come across as evasive if you actually do know the answer — add a reason or give a clearer response. Spelling note: double ㅆ — 글쎄요, not 글세요.

structuredNuance.t: 글쎄요는 특정 어원이 없는 감탄사(반응사)에 가깝다. 실제 뜻: 'hmm, well...' — 확신 없거나 결정을 보류하거나 부드럽게 거절하는 신호. 사실 모른다는 뜻이 아니라 입장이나 태도를 보류하는 말이다.
존댓말: 글쎄요 (누구에게나). 반말: 글쎄 (친구, 동생). 격식 상황: 잘 모르겠습니다가 더 자연스럽다. 상황: 요청에 확신 없을 때, 의견에 동의 못 할 때, 거절하기 애매할 때. 상사가 명확한 답변을 요구하는 상황에서는 글쎄요만 하면 무책임하게 들릴 수 있다.
글쎄요 vs 잘 모르겠어요: 글쎄요 = attitudinal hedging (I'm noncommittal / reluctant); 잘 모르겠어요 = honest factual ignorance ('I genuinely don't know'). 글쎄요 vs 음... : 음...은 단순한 생각하는 중 표시이고, 글쎄요는 보류/의구심 신호.
기본: 글쎄요. 반말: 글쎄. 확장: 글쎄요, 잘 모르겠는데요 (adds hedged 'I don't know'). 완화: 글쎄요... (trailing — implies 'I'd rather not'). 더 명확한 거절: 글쎄요, 좀 어려울 것 같아요.

1) Using 글쎄요 when asked a factual question you know the answer to — it signals uncertainty or reluctance; if you know, give the answer. 2) Treating it as casual 'whatever' — it's polite (ends in 요) and not dismissive when used alone. 3) Spelling: 글세요 is wrong — double ㅆ: 글쎄요.

mistakes: Treating 글쎄요 as a synonym for 'I don't know (a fact)' — for facts use 잘 모르겠어요; 글쎄요 is hesitation/doubt.
Using 글쎄요 to a superior who wants a definite answer — it can sound evasive; give a clearer response or add a reason.
Spelling it 글세요 — it's 글쎄요 with double ㅆ.

english: I'm not sure / I don't really know.
usage: polite; honest admission of uncertainty — works with anyone
반말; to a friend — same honest meaning
격식체; work settings, answering a superior formally
extension used when you share the uncertainty; 저도 = 'me too/either'
examples: A: 이 서류 어디다 제출해야 해요? / B: 저도 잘 모르겠어요. 담당자한테 여쭤봐야 할 것 같아요.
A: Where do we submit these documents? / B: I'm not sure either. I think we need to ask the person in charge.
A/B exchange: B admits uncertainty, then suggests a solution — the most natural way to respond when you don't know something at work
솔직히 아직 잘 모르겠어요. 좀 더 생각해 보고 말씀드릴게요.
Honestly, I'm not sure yet. Let me think it over and get back to you.
politely admitting uncertainty and offering a follow-up — shows the phrase can gracefully close a topic
이게 맞는 방향인지 잘 모르겠어요. 다 같이 한번 검토해 볼까요?
I'm not really sure if this is the right direction. Shall we all review it together?
expressing uncertainty about a choice, then proposing collaborative review — shows it can open a discussion
nuance: 잘 모르겠어요 is the natural, polite 'I'm not sure / I honestly don't know', used with anyone. Two things make it different from the bare 몰라요: first, 잘 ('well / properly') softens and naturalizes the admission — 'I don't really know well' is gentler than a flat 'I don't know'; second, the -겠- modal adds a layer of hedging or conjecture ('I guess I don't know'), making 모르겠어요 more polite and tentative than 몰라요. Together, 잘 모르겠어요 is the default softened 'I'm uncertain'. Casual is 잘 모르겠어; formal is 잘 모르겠습니다. The nearest alternative is 글쎄요 — the line: 잘 모르겠어요 genuinely reports lack of knowledge or certainty, while 글쎄요 is attitudinal hedging. Important: for not knowing a person (acquaintance), use 잘 몰라요 (present, factual), not 모르겠어요 — the -겠- marks inference or uncertainty, not factual ignorance of people.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 잘(well/properly) 모르겠어요(I don't seem to know) → 실제 뜻: 'I'm not really sure'. 두 가지 완화 장치: 잘 (부드럽게 만들기) + -겠- (추측/유보 표시). 이 둘 덕분에 bare 몰라요보다 훨씬 공손하다.
존댓말: 잘 모르겠어요 (누구에게나 자연스럽다). 반말: 잘 모르겠어. 격식: 잘 모르겠습니다. 특히 손님, 상사, 선생님에게 모른다고 할 때 bare 몰라요 대신 잘 모르겠어요나 잘 모르겠습니다를 써야 예의 바르다.

잘 모르겠어요 vs 글쎄요: 잘 모르겠어요 = honest report of lacking knowledge or certainty; 글쎄요 = noncommittal hedging (might know but is unsure whether to commit). 잘 모르겠어요 vs 몰라요: 몰라요 is blunter and can sound cold to strangers or superiors; 잘 모르겠어요 is softer.
기본: 잘 모르겠어요. 강조: 솔직히 잘 모르겠어요 ('honestly I'm not sure'). 해결책 추가: 잘 모르겠어요, 알아볼게요 ('not sure, let me find out'). 과거: 그때는 잘 몰랐어요 ('I didn't know at the time' — past uses 몰랐다).

1) Bare 몰라요 as a reply — it can sound blunt or cold, especially to someone you should be polite to; always soften to 잘 모르겠어요. 2) 잘 모르겠어요 for 'I don't know a person' — for not knowing a person use 잘 몰라요 (factual present); 모르겠어요 implies inference. 3) Dropping 잘 in polite contexts — 모르겠어요 alone is shorter but less warm; keep 잘 with strangers or seniors.

mistakes: Answering with a flat 몰라요 — it can sound blunt/cold; soften to 잘 모르겠어요.
Using 잘 모르겠어요 for 'I don't know a person' — for that use (잘) 몰라요; 모르겠어요 is about uncertainty/can't-tell.
Dropping 잘 in polite refusals of help — 잘 모르겠어요 is gentler than 모르겠어요 alone.

english: That doesn't seem right / I don't think that's okay.
usage: that's not really okay, I think
polite; the standard indirect way to voice disagreement or disapproval without a blunt 'no'
반말; to a close friend — still softened with 것 같아, not a harsh 아니야
격식체; work or formal setting — the most measured way to object
that's not really okay, is it?
extension seeking the listener's agreement on your objection — a tag-question form that shares responsibility
examples: 음, 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요. 다른 방법을 찾아봐요.
Hmm, I don't think that's okay. Let's look for another way.
softly rejecting an idea and suggesting an alternative — the combination is very Korean
A: 그냥 몰래 처리해 버릴까요? / B: 그렇게 하는 건 좀 아닌 것 같아요. 투명하게 하는 게 낫겠어요.
A: Should we just handle it secretly? / B: I don't think doing it that way is right. It'd be better to be transparent.
A/B exchange: B objects to unethical conduct using the indirect form — direct 틀렸어요 would be too confrontational
취지는 이해하는데, 그렇게까지 하는 건 좀 아닌 것 같아요.
I get the intention, but I don't think going that far is right.
acknowledging a valid purpose, then drawing a line at excessive methods — a very natural disagreement structure
nuance: 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 is the polite, face-saving way to object in Korean — 'that seems a bit wrong/inappropriate to me'. Three elements work together: 아니다 ('to not be so') provides the judgment; -ㄴ 것 같다 ('it seems') turns it into personal opinion rather than a verdict; and 좀 ('a bit') cushions the blow. Remove any of these and the phrase gets harsher. The casual form 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아 keeps the same hedges; the formal 그건 좀 아닌 것 같습니다 is for work. The nearest alternative is 저는 반대예요 — the dividing line: 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 is situational, indirect disapproval (a soft 'that's not right'); 저는 반대예요 is a clear on-the-record stance ('I oppose this'). The classic English-speaker mistake is being too direct — saying 그건 틀렸어요 ('that's wrong') or 안 돼요 for disagreement, which sounds confrontational and rude in Korean. Always keep 좀 and 것 같아요 to stay polite. Grammar note: it's 아닌 (adjective form from 아니다), not 안 인.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 그건(that) 좀(a bit) 아닌(not-so) 것 같아요(seems) → 실제 뜻: 'I don't think that's right/okay'. The literal meaning is face-saving by design — 'seems a bit off' rather than 'that's wrong'.
존댓말: 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 (누구에게나). 반말: 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아. 격식: 그건 좀 아닌 것 같습니다. 상황: 누군가의 제안이나 행동이 부적절하거나 과도하다고 느낄 때, 상대를 직접 비판하지 않고 간접적으로 이의를 제기할 때.

그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 vs 저는 반대예요: 아닌 것 같아요 = indirect, situational ('that seems off'); 반대예요 = explicit on-record objection ('I'm against it'). 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 vs 그건 좀 그래요: 그건 좀 그래요 is even softer/vaguer ('that's a bit...hmm') — maximum indirectness.
세 가지 완화 장치: 좀('a bit') + 아닌(adjective 'not-right') + 것 같아요('seems'). 모두 제거하면 그건 아니에요 — 훨씬 강하고 직접적이다. 확장: 그렇게까지 하는 건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 ('going that far seems a bit off').

1) 그건 틀렸어요 ('that's wrong') — too blunt and confrontational; soften to 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요. 2) 그건 안 돼요 ('that can't be done/not allowed') — this is a hard prohibition, much stronger than polite disagreement. 3) Writing 안 인 것 같아요 — wrong; the form from 아니다 is 아닌 것 같아요.

mistakes: Disagreeing with 그건 틀렸어요 ('that's wrong') — too blunt/confrontational; soften to 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요.
Dropping 좀 and 것 같아요 (그건 아니에요) — that's much harsher; the hedges are what make it polite.
Writing 안인 것 같아요 — the correct form from 아니다 is 아닌 것 같아요.

english: That's true, but... / That may be so, however...
usage: polite-neutral; concedes the other person's point before pivoting — works in both 반말 and 존댓말 contexts, since politeness lives in what follows
polite emphasis: adding 죠 makes the concession slightly warmer before the 'but'
격식체; meetings, written correspondence — -만 is a formal 'however'
extension reinforcing your reservation; 그래도 ('even so/still') signals you're not backing down
examples: 그렇긴 한데, 지금 당장 결정하기엔 좀 이른 것 같아요.
That's true, but I think it's a bit early to decide right now.
conceding, then gently pushing back on timing
A: 이게 더 빠른 방법이에요. / B: 그렇긴 한데, 오류가 날 가능성이 좀 있지 않을까요?
A: This method is faster. / B: That's true, but isn't there a chance of errors?
A/B exchange: B uses 그렇긴 한데 to acknowledge the advantage, then raises a concern — the most Korean way to push back politely
네, 그렇긴 한데, 그래도 한 번 더 확인해 보는 게 좋지 않을까요? 나중에 문제가 생기면 더 번거로울 테니까요.
Yes, that's true, but still, wouldn't it be better to double-check? It'll be more trouble if problems come up later.
fuller turn: concedes, pushes back with 그래도, then gives a reason — the complete structure
nuance: 그렇긴 한데 is the 'yes, but...' move in Korean — you grant the other person's point, then pivot to your reservation. The grammar: 그렇다 (to be so) + -기는 하다 (concession pattern, 'it IS so, granted') + -ㄴ데 (connective meaning 'but/and'). This -기는 하다 construction is the engine — it says 'I'll grant that it's true', and the -ㄴ데 suspends the sentence ready for the 'but'. Crucially, politeness lives in the clause that follows, not in 그렇긴 한데 itself — both 반말 and 존댓말 can use this exact form and only differ in the ending. The formal version is 그렇긴 합니다만. The nearest alternative is 그럴 수도 있죠 — the dividing line: 그렇긴 한데 actively concedes then disagrees; 그럴 수도 있죠 merely allows the possibility without necessarily disagreeing. English speakers often skip straight to 하지만/그러나 (the bare 'but'), which sounds argumentative without the softening concession first — 그렇긴 한데 is more diplomatic and culturally expected in Korean disagreement.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 그렇+긴(기는, 양보) 한(하다) 데(but/and) → 실제 뜻: 'granted that's true, but...'. The -기는 하다 pattern is the load-bearing concession mechanism — it says 'I'll grant it is so', setting up the 'but' that follows.
존댓말/반말: 그렇긴 한데 자체는 동일 — 그 뒤에 오는 말의 어미가 격식을 결정한다. 예: 그렇긴 한데, 좀 더 봐야 할 것 같아요 (존댓말) / 그렇긴 한데, 나는 좀 다르게 생각해 (반말). 격식: 그렇긴 합니다만.

그렇긴 한데 vs 그럴 수도 있죠: 그렇긴 한데 = concede then disagree; 그럴 수도 있죠 = allow a possibility neutrally (no pushback necessarily follows). 그렇긴 한데 vs 하지만: 하지만 is a direct 'but' with no concession softener — it can sound blunt.
기본: 그렇긴 한데. 강조: 그렇긴 한데, 그래도 ('true, but still'). 격식: 그렇긴 합니다만. 유사 패턴: 맞긴 맞는데 ('granted it's correct, but'), 좋긴 한데 ('it's good, but').

1) Jumping straight to 하지만/그러나 with no concession — sounds blunt and confrontational; use 그렇긴 한데 to cushion. 2) Spelling 그렇긴 한대 — the connective is -ㄴ데 (not -대): 그렇긴 한데. 3) Thinking -긴 has a future meaning — 그렇긴 한데 means 'it is so, granted, but', not anything about the future.

mistakes: Jumping to 하지만 with no concession — 그렇긴 한데 softens by conceding first; bare 하지만 sounds blunt.
Spelling the ending 한대 — the connective is -ㄴ데, so it's 그렇긴 한데.
Confusing 긴 (concession, =기는) with future — 그렇긴 한데 means 'it is so, granted, but', not anything future.

english: It's not great / I don't really like it.
usage: polite; mildly negative opinion — the standard way to say you're unimpressed without being rude
반말; to a friend — the most common casual negative verdict
I don't think it's that great
softer, hedged variant; 것 같아요 adds a layer of uncertainty, making it gentler than a bare 별로예요
past tense extension — used after actually trying something (food, movie, experience)
examples: 그 영화 어땠어요? — 솔직히 좀 별로였어요.
How was that movie? — Honestly, it wasn't that great.
A/B exchange: B gives a mildly negative verdict in past tense after having seen it — 별로였어요 is the natural post-experience form
맛은 괜찮은데 서비스는 좀 별로였어요.
The food was okay, but the service was kind of disappointing.
splitting a verdict — one part positive, one part 별로 — a very common review structure
음... 별로예요. 제 스타일이 아닌 것 같아요.
Hmm... it's not great. I don't think it's my style.
giving a mildly negative aesthetic verdict and offering a polite reason — 제 스타일이 아닌 것 같아요 softens the critique
nuance: 별로예요 is the everyday 'meh / not that great', a mildly negative opinion used with anyone in polite speech. 별로 originally means 'particularly / especially', and in its classic use it pairs with a negative verb: 별로 안 좋아요 ('not particularly good'), 별로 없어요 ('not particularly many'). In spoken Korean, 별로예요 has evolved to stand alone as 'it's not that great / I don't really like it' — the negative is implied. The casual form is 별로야; the hedged 별로인 것 같아요 is gentler. The nearest alternative is 그저 그래요 — the dividing line: 별로예요 leans clearly negative ('it's not good for me'), while 그저 그래요 is neutral 'so-so / average'. The top English-speaker mistakes: (1) spelling — it's 별로예요, never 별로에요 (after a pure-noun slot, the copula -이에요 contracts to 예요); (2) saying 별로 좋아요 — 별로 needs a negative; the correct form is 별로 안 좋아요 or stand-alone 별로예요; (3) treating 별로예요 as very strongly 'bad' — it's mild disapproval; for genuine dislike use 너무 별로예요 or 안 좋아요.

structuredNuance.t: 直譯: 별로(particularly/especially) + 예요(is/am/are) → 실제 뜻: 'it's not particularly good = it's meh'. 별로 comes from 별달리 ('particularly differently') and inherently implies 'not much' when used as a predicate standalone.
존댓말: 별로예요 / 별로인 것 같아요. 반말: 별로야. 격식: 별로 마음에 들지 않습니다 (more circumspect). 상황: 음식, 영화, 디자인, 서비스 등 어떤 것에 대한 평가를 물어봤을 때. 사람에 대해 직접 쓰면 무례할 수 있다 — 상대 앞에서 '그 사람 별로예요'는 피하자.

별로예요 vs 그저 그래요: 별로예요 = clearly negative ('I don't like it'); 그저 그래요 = neutral 'so-so / average'. 별로예요 vs 안 좋아요: 안 좋아요 is more direct and a bit stronger ('it's not good'). 별로 너무 싫어요: for strong dislike.
현재: 별로예요. 과거(경험 후): 별로였어요. 완화: 별로인 것 같아요. 강조: 진짜 별로예요 / 너무 별로예요. 결합: 별로 안 좋아요 (original structure — 별로 + negation + adjective).

1) Spelling 별로에요 — after the standalone 별로, the copula contracts to 예요: 별로예요. 2) 별로 좋아요 ('particularly good') — completely reverses the meaning; 별로 needs a negative: 별로 안 좋아요. 3) Treating 별로예요 as strongly 'bad' — it's mild; for strong dislike say 정말 별로예요 or 싫어요.

mistakes: Writing 별로에요 — the correct copula spelling here is 별로예요.
Saying 별로 좋아요 — 별로 needs a negative; use 별로 안 좋아요 or 별로예요.
Treating 별로예요 as strongly 'bad' — it's mild ('not great'); for strong dislike use 너무 별로예요 or 안 좋아요.

english: I think so / It seems that way.
usage: polite; softened confirmation — the standard hedge for opinions and assessments
반말; to a friend — same hedged quality
격식체; work settings, reporting, formal discussion
extension adding 아마 ('probably/maybe') for even more hedging when you're uncertain
examples: 오늘 비 올까요? — 그런 것 같아요. 아침부터 하늘이 어두웠거든요.
Will it rain today? — Seems like it. The sky has been dark since morning.
A/B exchange: B infers from visible evidence and adds the reason with -거든요 — how 그런 것 같아요 works with observable cues
다들 그 의견에 찬성하는 것 같아요. 분위기를 보니 그런 것 같아요.
Everyone seems to be for that idea. From the mood, it seems so.
reading a group situation and hedging the conclusion — the repeated 것 같아요 is natural in Korean
A: 이 방법이 더 효율적인 것 같죠? / B: 네, 그런 것 같아요. 시간이 많이 절약되는 것 같아요.
A: This method seems more efficient, right? / B: Yes, it does seem that way. Seems like it saves a lot of time.
A/B exchange: B confirms softly and adds an observation — notice both people use 것 같다, which is very natural in Korean conversation
nuance: 그런 것 같아요 ('it seems to be that way / so') is the hedged 'I think so', used constantly in Korean because -ㄴ/는 것 같다 is the core politeness device for expressing opinions tentatively rather than asserting flatly. Casual is 그런 것 같아; formal is 그런 것 같습니다. The nearest confident alternatives are 맞아요 and 그렇죠 — the dividing line: 그런 것 같아요 hedges ('seems so, I'm not fully certain'), while 맞아요/그렇죠 express confidence. Even when quite sure, Koreans often reach for 것 같아요 to avoid sounding pushy or presumptuous — this is a cultural politeness norm, not just uncertainty. The English-speaker tendency is to over-assert with 그래요/맞아요 where 그런 것 같아요 sounds more natural and modest. The reverse error is using 것 같다 for your own clear, immediate feelings when directness is actually expected (a doctor asking 'does it hurt?' — 아픈 것 같아요 can sound odd; 아파요 is more natural). Spacing: 그런 것 (two words), not 그런것.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 그런(such/that kind of) 것(thing) 같아요(seems) → 실제 뜻: 'it seems to be so / I think so'. The -ㄴ 것 같다 construction is the Korean opinion hedge: it frames your statement as a perception or tentative inference, not a certainty.
존댓말: 그런 것 같아요. 반말: 그런 것 같아. 격식: 그런 것 같습니다. 이 표현은 의견, 인상, 추론 등 모든 상황에서 자연스럽다. 그러나 '아파요?' 같은 직접적인 신체 반응 질문에는 직접 대답(아파요)이 더 자연스러울 수 있다.

그런 것 같아요 vs 맞아요/그렇죠: 것 같아요 = hedged ('seems so'); 맞아요/그렇죠 = confident ('right / exactly'). 그런 것 같아요 vs 그런 것 같습니다: same hedge, higher formality. 아마 그런 것 같아요 vs 그런 것 같아요: 아마 adds probability ('probably seems so').
완화: 아마 그런 것 같아요 (with 아마 = 'probably'). 강화: 확실히 그런 것 같아요 ('it definitely seems so'). 관련: ~ㄴ/는 것 같아요 패턴으로 어떤 형용사/동사와도 결합 가능 — 어려운 것 같아요, 갈 것 같아요 등.

1) Over-asserting with 맞아요/그래요 when unsure — 그런 것 같아요 is the natural modest hedge. 2) Writing 그런것 같아요 — 것 is a bound noun and MUST be spaced: 그런 것 같아요. 3) Overusing 것 같다 for strong personal feelings — for direct sensations (pain, hunger), stating directly (아파요, 배고파요) is more natural than hedging with 것 같다.

mistakes: Over-asserting with 맞아요/그래요 when unsure — 그런 것 같아요 is the natural hedge for 'I think so'.
Writing 그런것 같아요 — 것 is a bound noun and is spaced: 그런 것 같아요.
Confusing 그런 것 같다 (seems so) with 그렇다 (is so) — the 것 같다 version is tentative on purpose.

usage: that could be so / fair enough, it's possible
polite; acknowledging a possibility with open-minded concession — without committing for or against
반말; to a friend — same open concession
격식체; formal meetings or written responses
that might well be / I can see that now
extension: -겠네요 adds a nuance of 'I'm just now realizing that could be so' — warmer and more engaged
examples: 사람마다 느끼는 게 다르니까 그럴 수도 있죠.
People feel things differently, so that's possible.
conceding politely because individual experience varies — a common framing
A: 어쩌면 그 사람이 그냥 바빴던 것 같아요. / B: 그럴 수도 있죠. 너무 나쁘게 생각하지 마세요.
A: Maybe that person was just busy. / B: That could be. Don't think too badly of it.
A/B exchange: B uses 그럴 수도 있죠 to grant an innocent interpretation and then gives advice — a gentle, diplomatic response
그럴 수도 있죠. 근데 저라면 그 전에 한번 확인해 볼 것 같아요.
That's possible. But if it were me, I think I'd check first.
granting a possibility, then offering your own take — the classic 'that could be, but here's my view' pivot
nuance: 그럴 수도 있죠 says 'I'll grant that's a possibility' without committing to it — an open-minded, diplomatic concession. The grammar: 그렇다 → 그럴 (future/prospective modifier) + 수도 있다 ('it is possible, even') + 죠 (seeking mutual acknowledgment). 수도 is -도 ('even') attached to 수 ('possibility'), making it 'even possible' — slightly more concessive than bare 수 있다. Casual is 그럴 수도 있지; formal 그럴 수도 있습니다; the 그럴 수도 있겠네요 variant adds a warm 'I see that now'. The nearest alternative is 그렇긴 한데 — the key dividing line: 그럴 수도 있죠 grants a possibility neutrally (disagreement does not need to follow); 그렇긴 한데 concedes specifically to set up a 'but'. English speakers miss this distinction and force 아마 ('probably/maybe') everywhere, which gives a different nuance (likelihood estimate vs granting someone's point). Another trap: 가능해요 ('it's feasible/possible as an option') is about practical ability, not granting a conversational point. Spacing: 수 is a bound noun — 그럴 수도 있죠 (spaced), not 그럴수도 있죠.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 그럴(that way) 수도(possibility even) 있죠(there is, right?) → 실제 뜻: 'that could be so / fair enough, that's possible'. 수도 있다 = 'can even be' — the -도 ('even') makes it extra concessive.
존댓말: 그럴 수도 있죠. 반말: 그럴 수도 있지. 격식: 그럴 수도 있습니다. 상황: 상대방의 주장이나 추측에 가능성을 열어주면서도 명확히 동의하거나 반대하지 않을 때. 갈등을 완화할 때 특히 유용하다.

그럴 수도 있죠 vs 그렇긴 한데: 수도 있죠 = neutral concession (no pushback needed); 그렇긴 한데 = concede then disagree. 그럴 수도 있죠 vs 가능해요: 가능해요 = practical feasibility ('it's possible to do'); 그럴 수도 있죠 = granting someone's interpretation.
기본: 그럴 수도 있죠. 따뜻한 반응: 그럴 수도 있겠네요 ('I can see how that could be'). 반말: 그럴 수도 있지. 격식: 그럴 수도 있습니다. 확장: 그럴 수도 있죠, 하지만... (grant then pivot).

1) 가능해요 to mean 'that could be (in conversation)' — 가능하다 is practical feasibility; use 그럴 수도 있죠 for conversational concession. 2) 그럴수도 있죠 (no space) — 수 is a bound noun: 그럴 수도 있죠. 3) Using 아마 everywhere for 'maybe' — 아마 estimates likelihood; 그럴 수도 있죠 grants someone else's raised possibility.

mistakes: Saying 가능해요 to mean 'that could be (in conversation)' — 가능하다 is about feasibility; for granting a point use 그럴 수도 있죠.
Writing 그럴수도 있죠 — 수 is a bound noun and is spaced: 그럴 수도 있죠.
Forcing 아마 ('maybe/probably') in its place — 아마 estimates likelihood; 그럴 수도 있죠 concedes a possibility someone raised.

usage: polite; clear on-the-record opposition — use when you need your stance to be known
반말; to a close friend or peer
격식체; business meetings, votes, formal decisions
extension naming what you oppose — note the particle 에, not 을/를
examples: 미안하지만 저는 반대예요. 리스크가 너무 클 것 같아서요.
Sorry, but I'm against it. I think the risk would be too high.
polite opposition softened with 미안하지만 and a reason (-어서요) — the recommended structure
다들 찬성하시는 것 같은데, 저는 솔직히 반대예요. 이유를 말씀드려도 될까요?
Everyone seems to be in favor, but honestly I'm against it. May I explain my reasons?
voicing a minority objection in a group, then asking permission to elaborate — shows how to use 반대예요 without seeming stubborn
A: 이 안건 찬반 의견 주세요. / B: 저는 반대입니다. 예산 대비 효과가 불확실하기 때문입니다.
A: Please share your opinions on this agenda item. / B: I'm opposed. The return on the budget is uncertain.
formal meeting exchange: B uses 반대합니다 and gives a business reason — the expected register in a work setting
nuance: 저는 반대예요 is the explicit, on-the-record 'I'm against it', used when you want your opposition known — typical in meetings, planning sessions, or group decisions. 반대[反對] means 'opposition' (literally 'against / facing the other way'); its antonym is 찬성[贊成] ('approval / being for'). Casual is 나는 반대야; formal is 저는 반대합니다, which is standard in business Korean. The nearest alternative is 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 — the dividing line: 저는 반대예요 is explicit and committed (you're registering a position), while 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요 is indirect and situational (a gentle 'that seems off'). Because clear opposition can feel blunt in Korean social settings, it's conventional to soften: lead with 미안하지만 ('sorry, but') or follow with a reason ending in -아서요/-어서요. The particle rule: you oppose something using 에 (그 의견에 반대예요), not 을/를 — the English phrase 'oppose something' misleads learners into the object marker. Also distinguish 반대 from 반대로 ('on the contrary / in reverse'), which is an adverb about direction.

structuredNuance.t: 反對(한자): 반(against) + 대(facing) = 'opposing'. 저는 반대예요 = 'I stand in opposition'. This is a committed stance, not a vague feeling of discomfort — it registers you as being against a proposal.
존댓말: 저는 반대예요 (누구에게나). 반말: 나는 반대야 (친구). 격식: 저는 반대합니다 (회의, 공식 발표). 가장 자연스러운 상황: 회의에서 의견 표명, 팀 결정, 투표. 부드럽게 하려면 미안하지만을 앞에 붙이거나 이유를 뒤에 덧붙인다.

저는 반대예요 vs 그건 좀 아닌 것 같아요: 반대예요 = explicit registered opposition (you're staking a position); 아닌 것 같아요 = gentle indirect disapproval. 반대예요 vs 저는 동의 안 해요: 동의 안 해요 = 'I don't agree' (less formal, based on 동의); 반대예요 is the cleaner native expression.
완화: 미안하지만 저는 반대예요 + 이유. 격식: 저는 반대합니다. 부분 반대: 일부에는 동의하지만 이 부분은 반대예요. 반의어: 저는 찬성이에요 / 찬성합니다.

1) 그 의견을 반대예요 (wrong particle) — 반대하다 takes 에: 그 의견에 반대예요. 2) No cushioning — direct opposition can feel abrupt; add 미안하지만 or a reason. 3) Confusing 반대 with 반대로 — 반대로 means 'on the contrary / in reverse' (an adverb about direction), not 'I oppose'.

mistakes: Saying 그 의견을 반대예요 — 반대(하다) takes 에: 그 의견에 반대예요.
Opposing bluntly with no cushion — add 미안하지만 or a reason (-아서요) so it doesn't sound combative.
Confusing 반대 with 반대로 — 반대로 means 'on the contrary/in reverse'; for 'I'm against it' it's 저는 반대예요.

usage: polite; warmly endorsing someone's suggestion — the most natural compliment for an idea
반말; to a close friend — same warmth, lower register
격식/경어; toward a senior or customer — the -시- honorific marks deference
extension with -네요: adds mild surprise or fresh realization — 'oh, that IS a good idea'
examples: 같이 점심 먹을까요? — 좋은 생각이에요! 어디로 갈까요?
Shall we have lunch together? — Great idea! Where should we go?
A/B exchange: B enthusiastically endorses and immediately moves forward — shows how the phrase opens collaborative planning
회의를 오전으로 옮기자고요? 좋은 생각이에요. 그 시간대가 더 집중이 잘 될 것 같아요.
Move the meeting to the morning? Good idea. I think we can focus better at that time.
endorsing and backing it with a reason — 이에요 + reason is a natural work-chat response pattern
A: 미리 예약해 두면 어때요? / B: 오, 좋은 생각이에요! 나중에 줄 서는 거 싫거든요.
A: What if we make a reservation in advance? / B: Oh, that's a great idea! I hate waiting in line later.
A/B exchange: B reacts with -네요 energy (mild pleased surprise) via 좋은 생각이에요 + personal reason
nuance: 좋은 생각이에요 ('that's a good thought/idea') is the warm, natural way to praise a suggestion in Korean — used with anyone in polite speech. The components: 좋은 (adjective modifier from 좋다 'good') + 생각 ('thought/idea') + 이에요 (copula). Adding -네요 (좋은 생각이네요) adds a tone of pleasant discovery — 'oh, that IS a good idea'. Casual is 좋은 생각이야; the honorific 좋은 생각이십니다 is used with seniors or customers. The nearest alternative is 좋아요 — the dividing line: 좋은 생각이에요 specifically compliments the idea as clever or sensible; 좋아요 is general assent ('sounds good, fine, okay') without the compliment. For accepting a request you don't particularly need to praise, 좋아요 works; for genuinely endorsing someone's creative suggestion, 좋은 생각이에요 is warmer. English speakers sometimes say 좋은 아이디어예요 (using the loanword 아이디어), which is perfectly common in Korea, but 좋은 생각이에요 is the more natively Korean phrasing. Watch the copula: after 생각 (consonant ending), the copula is 이에요, not 에요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 좋은(good) 생각(thought/idea) 이에요(is) → 실제 뜻: 'that's a good idea'. It actively praises the quality of the idea — not just 'okay' but 'that is genuinely good thinking'.
존댓말: 좋은 생각이에요 (누구에게나). 반말: 좋은 생각이야. 경어: 좋은 생각이십니다 (선생님, 상사, 손님). 상황: 누군가의 제안이나 아이디어에 반응할 때. 일상적인 계획(식사, 여행, 일정)부터 직장 회의까지 모두 자연스럽다.

좋은 생각이에요 vs 좋아요: 생각이에요 = compliments the idea specifically ('that's a smart suggestion'); 좋아요 = general assent ('sounds fine / okay'). 좋은 생각이에요 vs 좋은 아이디어예요: 아이디어 is the loanword variant — equally common in modern Korean, slightly more casual or youthful.
기본: 좋은 생각이에요. 발견/감탄: 좋은 생각이네요 (with -네요 for fresh realization). 반말: 좋은 생각이야. 경어: 좋은 생각이십니다. 강조: 정말 좋은 생각이에요 / 아주 좋은 생각인 것 같아요.

1) 좋은 생각에요 — after 생각 (consonant-ending noun) the copula is 이에요: 좋은 생각이에요. 2) 좋는 생각 — 좋다 is an adjective; the correct modifier is 좋은, not 좋는. 3) Defaulting to 좋아요 when you want to compliment the idea — 좋아요 is general assent; 좋은 생각이에요 is the warmer, idea-praising phrase.

mistakes: Writing 좋은 생각에요 — after 생각 (ends in a consonant) the copula is 이에요: 좋은 생각이에요.
Saying 좋는 생각 — 좋다 is an adjective, so the modifier is 좋은, not 좋는.
Reducing it to bare 좋아요 when you mean to praise the idea — 좋아요 is general assent; 좋은 생각이에요 compliments the idea itself.

english: What I mean is... / My point is...
usage: polite; used to clarify, restate, or rescue your point — especially after being misunderstood
반말; same function, lower register — to a friend or peer
격식/경어; toward a senior, customer, or in formal writing — raises the politeness of your own speech
what I mean is, it's not that
the most common extension: correcting a misunderstanding head-on before restating the real point
examples: 아니, 제 말은 그게 아니라, 미리 준비하자는 거예요.
No, what I mean is, it's not that — I'm saying we should prepare in advance.
the most typical use: 제 말은 그게 아니라 + the corrected intent — rescuing a misunderstood point
A: 저 그렇게까지 하라는 말이에요? / B: 아니요, 제 말은 방향만 잡아 두자는 거예요.
A: Are you saying I should go that far? / B: No, what I mean is, let's just set the direction.
A/B exchange: B uses 제 말은 to narrow the misunderstood scope — very natural in Korean work discussions
제 말은, 지금 당장 결정할 필요는 없다는 거예요. 시간이 좀 있잖아요.
What I'm saying is, there's no need to decide right now. We have some time.
clarifying a misread urgency without a conflict — shows 제 말은 without 그게 아니라 when no direct correction is needed
nuance: 제 말은 ('as for my words / what I'm saying is') is the go-to repair phrase in Korean — you use it to reframe, clarify, or rescue your intended meaning when you've been misunderstood or when your point hasn't landed. 제 = humble 'my'; 말 = 'words / speech'; 은 = topic particle ('as for'). The casual form is 내 말은; 제 말씀은 raises deference and is used toward seniors or customers. The most natural extension is 제 말은 그게 아니라 ('my point isn't that — it's...'), which corrects a misreading before restating. The nearest alternative is 그러니까 ('so / what I'm saying is') — the dividing line: 그러니까 reframes or continues your reasoning as a logical next step; 제 말은 explicitly re-centers on YOUR intended meaning after a misunderstanding. English speakers reach for 제가 의미하는 건 ('what I mean is' translated literally), which is unnatural in spoken Korean. Another mistake: dropping the topic particle 은 (제 말 그게 아니라) — keep 은 for the frame to work.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 제(my/humble) 말(words/speech) 은(as for) → 실제 뜻: 'as for what I'm saying / what I mean is'. It is a repair opener — it signals 'let me re-anchor what I actually intended'. Most powerful before 그게 아니라 ('it's not that').
존댓말: 제 말은 (누구에게나). 반말: 내 말은 (친구, 동생). 경어/격식: 제 말씀은 (선생님, 상사, 손님). 상황: 상대가 자신의 말을 잘못 이해했을 때, 요점을 다시 강조할 때, 오해를 바로잡을 때.

제 말은 vs 그러니까: 그러니까 = 'so / in other words' (continues/reframes reasoning); 제 말은 = 're-centers on MY intended meaning' (usually after misunderstanding). 제 말은 그게 아니라 vs 그게 아니에요: 그게 아니에요 is a blunt correction; 제 말은 그게 아니라 is gentler and explains rather than just denies.
기본: 제 말은 + [내용]. 수정형: 제 말은 그게 아니라 + [진짜 의도]. 반말: 내 말은 그게 아니라... 경어: 제 말씀은 그게 아니라... 강조: 제 말은 결국 이거예요 ('my point comes down to this').

1) 제가 의미하는 건 — a literal calque of 'what I mean is'; unnatural in spoken Korean; use 제 말은. 2) 내 말은 with someone you must be polite to — switch to 제 말은 or 제 말씀은. 3) Dropping the topic particle (제 말 그게 아니라) — keep 은: 제 말은 그게 아니라.

mistakes: Calquing 'I mean' as 제가 의미하는 건 — unnatural; say 제 말은.
Using 내 말은 with someone you must be polite to — switch to 제 말은 (or 제 말씀은).
Dropping the topic particle (제 말 그게 아니라) — keep 은: 제 말은 그게 아니라.
